short: An Israeli tank designed around crew survival, with the engine at the front.
full:
After Britain declined to sell Israel the Chieftain in 1969, Israel Tal directed the design of a national tank. The Merkava entered service in 1979 with an unusual layout: the engine and transmission sit in front of the crew as an additional layer of protection, and the rear of the hull holds a compartment with a clamshell door, used for ammunition stowage, casualty evacuation or carrying a handful of infantry. It fought first in Lebanon in 1982.

The emphasis on crew survivability reflected an army for which trained crews were scarcer than vehicles. Later marks brought a 120 mm smoothbore, modular armour and, from 2011, the Trophy active protection system, which shoots down incoming anti-tank missiles and has since been bought by the United States for the Abrams. Around 2,000 have been built in four main marks; the Merkava has never been exported in quantity and remains in Israeli service.
